title: Zoonotic Hybridization of Schistosoma bovis and Schistosoma haematobium: Implications for Human Morbidity and the Unexplored Territory of Appendiceal Schistosomiasis.
abstract: African schistosomiasis control has traditionally focused on human-only transmission. However, emerging molecular evidence demonstrates widespread hybridization between the human parasite Schistosoma haematobium and the livestock parasite Schistosoma bovis, challenging the traditional anthroponotic paradigm and reshaping our understanding of parasite virulence and tissue distribution. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to synthesize evidence on S. haematobium × S. bovis hybridization, zoonotic multi-host transmission pathways, and associated clinical manifestations, with a particular focus on the unexamined pathology of appendiceal schistosomiasis. Out of 847 records, 15 high-quality studies met the eligibility criteria. Genotypic evidence confirms widespread bidirectional introgressive hybridization across West Africa, with hybrid prevalence reaching up to 100% in some human cohorts. One Health investigations support a multi-host cycle where S. bovis spills over from cattle to humans, pairs with S. haematobium, and propagates through Bulinus snails via human-to-human transmission. Clinically, hybrid infections are linked to altered morbidity profiles, notably increased hepatomegaly and reduced post-treatment resolution of bladder lesions. While histopathological reviews show that schistosomal appendicitis affects up to 4.15% of appendectomies in endemic areas, every identified study relied solely on microscopy without molecular characterization. Zoonotic hybrid schistosomes alter human clinical profiles and transmission dynamics across Africa. However, their specific involvement in ectopic pathologies like appendiceal schistosomiasis remains entirely unknown, highlighting a critical research gap at the intersection of molecular epidemiology and surgical pathology.

title: Structural basis of avian-to-human receptor-binding adaptation in H9Ny influenza A virus hemagglutinin.
abstract: The receptor-binding specificity of influenza A virus (IAV) hemagglutinin (HA) is a major determinant for viral host tropism, enabling interspecies transmission. The molecular determinants for receptor-binding properties of HAs vary among different IAV subtypes. In this study, we performed a comprehensive analysis on the receptor-binding determinants of IAV subtype H9 HA and found that the receptor-binding characteristics of H9 subtype influenza viruses have exhibited temporal variations over decades. Q226L (hydrophobicity switch) substitution in the 220-loop is the key determinant for H9 subtype HA to acquire human receptor-binding preference. The amino acid residues of the 130-loop greatly affect the binding of HA protein to canonical receptors. Organoid infection models demonstrate that all three representative viral strains could infect human bronchial epithelial organoids. These findings increase our understanding of the molecular determinants of receptor-binding properties of different HA subtypes and call for the surveillance and response to potential influenza outbreaks, or even epidemics/pandemics.IMPORTANCEInfluenza A virus (IAV) subtype H9 poses persistent zoonotic spillover risks due to its adaptive receptor-binding capacity, yet the molecular determinants remain incompletely defined. This study systematically characterizes the receptor-binding determinants of H9 hemagglutinin over decades of viral evolution and identifies two critical functional domains: the 220-loop residue Q226L substitution, which serves as the key mutation conferring human receptor-binding preference, and the 130-loop residues that predominantly modulate canonical receptor-binding affinity. Functional assays using human bronchial epithelial organoids further confirm the robust human infection ability of prevalent H9 viral strains. These findings clarify the molecular mechanisms underlying H9 IAV host tropism and adaptive evolution, provide critical theoretical evidence for targeted influenza surveillance and pandemic preparedness against emerging H9 influenza outbreaks.

title: Tracking respiratory syncytial virus dynamics in wastewater during the 2024-2025 season in Switzerland.
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for a substantial health burden worldwide, particularly among children and older adults. In 2023, novel immunoprophylactic interventions for RSV were approved, underscoring the need to monitor circulating RSV lineages and detect mutations that could compromise intervention effectiveness. Here, we implemented wastewater-based genomic RSV surveillance by integrating digital PCR and amplicon-based sequencing within Switzerland's national wastewater monitoring program. We tracked RSV subtypes and individual mutations across the 2024-2025 peak season in six Swiss cities. RSV-A and RSV-B co-circulated nationwide, and both exhibited similar epidemiological dynamics estimated from their subtype-specific effective reproduction numbers. No previously reported F protein mutations relevant to prophylaxis efficacy were identified. Genetic diversity analysis of wastewater-derived sequences reflected patterns previously reported in clinical data, with higher diversity in RSV-A than RSV-B, and greater variability in the G compared to the F gene. These findings demonstrate the potential of wastewater-based RSV surveillance for monitoring RSV dynamics and diversity and establish a national baseline for RSV evolution during the first season following vaccine implementation in Switzerland.IMPORTANCERespiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common respiratory virus that can cause serious illness in vulnerable populations. The recent development of RSV immunoprophylaxis products has increased the importance of monitoring viral evolution. Standard surveillance based on clinical testing captures only a fraction of infections. Our findings demonstrate that wastewater-based genomic surveillance, using regularly collected samples throughout the peak RSV season, can provide a cost-effective and representative picture of viral dynamics. Expanding this approach into future RSV seasons and across a broader geographic scope will enable continuous tracking of viral evolution, including detection of novel mutations, which is particularly important given the widespread introduction of new vaccines and preventive treatments.

title: Molecular Epidemiology of Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 High-Pathogenicity Avian Influenza in South Africa, 2025-2026.
abstract: The panzootic Goose/Guangdong clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 high-pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) virus severely threatens global poultry industries and wildlife conservation. Following two major southern African epizootics between 2017 and 2023, a new clade 2.3.4.4b outbreak emerged in South Africa in June 2025. To establish evolutionary and transmission dynamics, representative viruses from commercial poultry and diverse wild bird populations were sequenced and analyzed via maximum likelihood (ML) and time-scaled Bayesian maximum clade credibility (MCC) phylogenetic trees to determine sub-genotype assignments and track virus dispersal. Specific genetic markers were evaluated. Phylogenetic analysis of 125 novel genome sequences revealed a distinct introduction of genotype EA-2024-DI.2 from Europe. While commercial poultry cases were significantly lower than during previous waves, there were sizable outbreaks in colony-breeding coastal seabirds. A specific coastal seabird lineage persisted through the summer and propagated northward into Namibia, mirroring past epizootics. The findings suggest an emerging 4-year cyclical trend of northern hemisphere incursions. Furthermore, climate-driven water availability for wild duck vectors likely triggered an unprecedented reverse viral migration from the southern coastal region back into South Africa's northern interior. These findings provide vital baselines for future epidemiological risk assessments, highlighting an urgent regional priority for establishing coordinated wild bird surveillance alongside targeted vaccination strategies.

title: Spatio-temporal Moran dynamics in continuous media.
abstract: Understanding how natural selection unfolds across space and time is a central problem in evolutionary biology. Classical models such as the Moran process capture stochastic birth-death dynamics in structured populations, while reaction-diffusion equations like the Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov (FKPP) equation describe deterministic wavelike spread. In this work, we bridge these perspectives by deriving partial differential equations for the spatio-temporal limit of Moran dynamics in continuous media. Our model incorporates two distinct fitness components: fecundity (birth rate) and viability (death rate). We demonstrate that the resulting selective wave speeds differ substantially in spatial Moran birth-death (BD), Moran death-birth (DB) and FKPP dynamics. When fecundity drives the dynamics, we observe that the selective waves decelerate for the BD process, whereas in the DB process the wave propagates with a higher, constant speed. By contrast, when viability drives the process, the DB wave accelerates, while the BD and FKPP waves maintain comparable constant speeds. We extend the framework to heterogeneous media, represented as weighted lattice graphs in one or two dimensions. We derive a continuous-space analogue of isothermal graphs and establish that the isothermality condition corresponds to the conservation of a local current.

title: Uncovering Newcastle disease virus dynamics in Northern Nigeria: insights from an epidemiological survey in unvaccinated village poultry.
abstract: Newcastle disease virus (NDV) remains a major constraint to village and backyard poultry production in Nigeria, where limited vaccination and low biosecurity may facilitate sustained virus circulation. This study investigated the serological and molecular epidemiology of NDV in unvaccinated village poultry across Plateau, Bauchi, and Kano States, northern Nigeria. A cross-sectional survey was conducted in 502 villages between 2020 and 2024. Serum samples (n = 3,999) and pooled tracheal/cloacal swabs (n = 2,113) were collected from extensively managed backyard poultry. After excluding flocks with a history of NDV vaccination, 3,831 sera from 481 villages were analyzed using indirect ELISA. Pooled swabs were screened by real-time RT-PCR and positive samples were sequenced for phylogenetic relatedness. Bird-level seropositivity was 16% in Plateau, 22% in Bauchi, and 22% in Kano, while 68-80% of villages in the three states had at least one seropositive bird, indicating widespread NDV exposure. Seroprevalence varied by species, flock size, and state, with turkeys generally showing higher exposure. Small and medium-sized flocks exhibited higher seropositivity than large flocks. Biosecurity measures, including fencing and shelter, were not significantly associated (p > 0.05) with seropositivity. Of 2,113 pooled swab samples, 950 tested positive for NDV RNA. Phylogenetic analysis revealed widespread circulation of lentogenic genotype I.1.1, closely related to the NDV-I2 vaccine strain, alongside velogenic genotype XIV.2, detected in chickens, ducks, and turkeys across all states. A velogenic pigeon-associated genotype XXI.1.1 was also identified in Bauchi State. These findings revealed widespread NDV circulation in rural poultry systems across northern Nigeria, highlighting the need for improved surveillance, strengthened biosecurity, and adoption of genotype-matched vaccination strategies.

title: Hidden diversity and complex transmission networks of Taeniidae and Dipylidiidae tapeworms in the Western Balkans revealed by mitochondrial markers.
abstract: Cestodes of the families Taeniidae and Dipylidiidae constitute a neglected but epidemiologically important group of parasites, including species of veterinary and zoonotic relevance. In the Western Balkans, their molecular epidemiology, host range, and transmission dynamics remain largely unresolved, limiting accurate assessment of their ecological and public health significance. We conducted a large-scale molecular survey of cestodes collected from a broad spectrum of definitive (dogs, domestic cats, brown bears, European badgers, European hedgehogs, European wildcats, golden jackals, grey wolves, red foxes, and stone martens) and intermediate hosts (dog, goats, pigs, sheep, roe deer, and wild boars) across Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina over a 10-year period (2014-2024). A total of 254 cestode specimens comprising adult cestodes and larval stages were analysed using mitochondrial markers (cox1 and nad1), followed by phylogenetic and haplotype analyses to resolve species identity, genetic diversity, and transmission patterns. We provide the first comprehensive molecular evidence of nine taeniid species and multiple dipylidiid lineages circulating in the region. Generalist carnivores, particularly red foxes and golden jackals, emerged as key hubs of parasite diversity, harboring the highest number of taxa and linking multiple transmission cycles. Several species (e.g., Taenia hydatigena, T. krabbei, T. martis) exhibited broad host associations, while phylogenetic analyses revealed extensive gene flow across geographic boundaries, indicating a continuous regional transmission system. Notably, we detected previously unrecognized genetic divergence within Taenia pisiformis and Joyeuxiella spp., suggesting cryptic diversity. Additionally, both canine and feline genotypes of Dipylidium caninum were identified, including evidence of cross-host transmission. The detection of zoonotic species such as T. crassiceps and T. martis further highlights the relevance of these parasite communities at the human-animal interface. Our findings redefine the epidemiological landscape of cestodes in the Western Balkans, demonstrating that parasite transmission operates within highly interconnected, cross-border networks driven by generalist carnivores and shared ecological niches. This study establishes a critical molecular baseline and provides strong evidence that southeastern Europe represents an active hotspot of cestode diversity and transmission. Integrating wildlife into surveillance frameworks is essential for accurate risk assessment within a One Health context.

title: Morphological and molecular characterization of Dicrocoelium dendriticum and Dicrocoelium chinensis in small ruminants from Inner Mongolia, China.
abstract: Dicrocoeliosis is a parasitic liver disease of domestic and wild ruminants and can also affect humans, resulting in animal-production losses and potential public health concerns. This study aimed to identify Dicrocoelium dendriticum and Dicrocoelium chinensis in small ruminants from Inner Mongolia using integrated morphological and molecular approaches. Liver samples from 80 sheep and 280 goats were collected at slaughterhouses, and recovered flukes were subjected to morphometric examination and acetocarmine staining. Molecular identification based on ITS-2 and COX-1 sequences confirmed D. dendriticum in goats from Ordos and D. chinensis in sheep from Hinggan League. The prevalence was 5.0% for D. dendriticum in goats and 26.25% for D. chinensis in sheep. The testes were arranged in tandem in D. dendriticum and were opposed in D. chinensis. The sampled D. chinensis population had a greater maximum body width and larger oral and ventral suckers, whereas the distance from the anterior end to the point of maximum body width was greater in the sampled D. dendriticum population. ITS-2 and COX-1 sequences formed two well-supported species-specific clades. COX-1 analysis identified six haplotypes in D. chinensis, dominated by Hap_30 (67.4%), and 29 haplotypes in D. dendriticum, dominated by Hap_2 (23.2%). ITS-2 was useful for discriminating D. dendriticum and D. chinensis but showed limited resolution for intraspecific variation, whereas COX-1 provided greater resolution for haplotype analysis. Because host species and geographic region were confounded in the sampling design, differences between the sampled populations should not be attributed solely to host or geography. These findings provide baseline data for molecular epidemiology, genetic diversity assessment, and surveillance of Dicrocoelium spp. in Inner Mongolia.
journal: Veterinary parasitology, regional studies and reports

title: Molecular epidemiology, virulence gene profiles, and clinical outcomes of bovine Cryptosporidium in Türkiye.
abstract: Cryptosporidium spp. are major causes of neonatal calf diarrhea and represent a zoonotic concern. This study investigated Cryptosporidium occurrence, GP60 subtype distribution, and selected virulence-associated gene targets in bovine field samples from Türkiye. Fecal samples were collected from 83 diarrheic calves aged 5-30 days from 20 farms; after 16 of the sampled calves subsequently died, their respective asymptomatic dams were additionally sampled as an outcome-dependent, calf-associated group rather than as an independent control group. All 99 samples were screened by Kinyoun acid-fast staining, and the 76 microscopy-positive samples were subsequently subjected to SSU 18S rRNA nested PCR. Ten virulence-associated gene targets were screened by PCR, and GP60 subtyping was performed for all PCR-confirmed samples. Oocyst-like structures were detected in 76/99 samples (76.8%), and 74/76 (97.4%) microscopy-positive samples were confirmed by PCR. GP60 sequence analysis identified two C. parvum IIa subtype patterns: IIaA13G2R1 (58/74, 78.4%) and IIaA14G1R1 (16/74, 21.6%). In this dataset, IIaA13G2R1 was detected in all fatal calf cases and their asymptomatic dams, whereas IIaA14G1R1 was observed only among non-fatal diarrheic calves. GP60, COWP, Cp15, TRAP-C1, HSP70, HSP90, and aminopeptidase-like metalloprotease were detected in all 74 PCR-confirmed samples; cryptopain and cryptostatin were each detected in 65/74 samples (87.8%), and CDPK in 58/74 samples (78.4%). Among the variably detected targets, CDPK showed an exploratory association with calf outcome; however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously. Apart from previous PCR-based work targeting COWP and Cp15, this study provides the first broader PCR-based profile of selected virulence-associated gene targets in bovine Cryptosporidium field samples from Türkiye. These findings represent preliminary molecular associations and should not be interpreted as evidence of gene expression, functional virulence, or causality.
journal: Veterinary parasitology, regional studies and reports
